input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-331: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments are an integral part of the course. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[mit-computer-vision]
Computer vision connects image evidence to models of geometry, appearance, motion, objects, and scenes. Projective geometry relates three-dimensional points to image coordinates. Appearance models describe how lighting, material, and viewpoint affect measured pixels. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses. Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships. A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift.

[opencv-documentation]
Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values. Filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement. Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Motion methods compare observations across time. Results depend on sampling, illumination, noise, training data, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

[rit-csci-331]
An introduction to the theories and algorithms used to create artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Topics include search algorithms, logic, planning, machine learning, and applications from areas such as computer vision, robotics, and natural language processing. Programming assignments are an integral part of the course. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205) or equivalent courses. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have taken CSCI-630. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: An AI system pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule.
beats.example: A self-driving car system defines its task as detecting pedestrians, represents them as bounding boxes, assumes clear daylight conditions, uses labeled training data for supervision, and applies a confidence threshold to decide whether to h
beats.title: Foundations of AI System Architecture
beats.visualDirection: Show a five-step pipeline diagram labeled Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, and Decision Rule. Annotate each node with a brief label and connect them with arrows to show sequential flow.

beats.claim: Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays.
beats.example: A 100x100 color image is stored as a 30000-element array where each triplet corresponds to red, green, and blue pixel values.
beats.title: Image Representation in Computer Vision
beats.visualDirection: Display a small grid of pixels transforming into a matrix of numbers. Highlight one pixel and show its RGB values as a numeric triplet.

beats.claim: Color conversion changes the coordinate representation of pixel values, and filtering combines neighboring samples to smooth, sharpen, or detect structure.
beats.example: Converting an RGB image to grayscale reduces three channels to one, simplifying edge detection. A Gaussian filter smooths noisy pixel values by averaging adjacent samples.
beats.title: Color Conversion and Filtering
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison: original noisy image, grayscale version, and filtered image. Use arrows to indicate the color conversion and filtering steps.

beats.claim: Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns, while calibration estimates camera parameters needed for geometric measurement.
beats.example: SIFT features identify keypoints like corners and edges. Camera calibration maps real-world distances to pixel coordinates using known reference points.
beats.title: Feature Detection and Calibration
beats.visualDirection: Draw a grid of detected feature points on an image. Overlay a calibration grid showing how real-world distances map to image coordinates.

beats.claim: Geometric transforms map coordinates between image representations, and segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories.
beats.example: Perspective transform corrects a tilted photo. Foreground segmentation isolates moving objects from a static background.
beats.title: Geometric Transforms and Segmentation
beats.visualDirection: Show a distorted image transforming into a straight, aligned image. Highlight segmented regions with different colors.

beats.claim: Motion estimation compares observations across frames, and object recognition maps visual evidence to object hypotheses.
beats.example: Optical flow tracks pixel movement between video frames. A face detector classifies detected regions as human faces based on learned patterns.
beats.title: Motion Estimation and Object Recognition
beats.visualDirection: Display two consecutive video frames with arrows showing pixel movement. Annotate detected faces with bounding boxes and labels.

beats.claim: Scene understanding combines objects, layout, and contextual relationships to interpret complex environments.
beats.example: A kitchen scene is understood by recognizing a stove, a pot, and a person standing near the stove, establishing spatial and functional relationships.
beats.title: Scene Understanding and Context
beats.visualDirection: Show a kitchen image with labeled objects and lines connecting them to indicate relationships (e.g., person near stove).

beats.claim: Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift to ensure reliable performance.
beats.example: An AI model is tested with images taken at different angles, under bright and dim light, with partial occlusions, and from different camera types.
beats.title: Evaluation and Robustness Testing
beats.visualDirection: Display a 2x2 grid of test images varying in viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Annotate each with the tested condition.

beats.claim: A rigorous pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule, and evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift
beats.example: Before deploying a vision system, verify: 1) Task is clearly defined, 2) Representation matches data format, 3) Assumptions are validated, 4) Supervision data is representative, 5) Decision rule is calibrated, 6) Evaluation covers viewpoint
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Create a checklist graphic with six boxes. Check off each item as it relates to the pipeline components and evaluation criteria.

beats.claim: An AI system pipeline states the task, representation, assumptions, supervision, and decision rule.
beats.example: A self-driving car system defines its task as detecting pedestrians, represents them as bounding boxes, assumes clear daylight conditions, uses labeled training data for supervision, and applies a confidence threshold to decide whether to h

beats.visualDirection: Show a five-step pipeline diagram labeled Task, Representation, Assumptions, Supervision, and Decision Rule. Annotate each node with a brief label and connect them with arrows to show sequential flow.

input.text: Examine the tradeoffs in Motion Estimation and Object Recognition, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Motion estimation compares observations across frames. Consider this worked case: Optical flow tracks pixel movement between video frames. A face detector classifies detected regions as human faces based on learned patterns. On screen, display two consecutive video frames with arrows showing pixel movement. Annotate detected faces with bounding boxes and labels. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Now define Image Representation in Computer Vision precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Computer vision pipelines represent images as numeric arrays. Consider this worked case: A 100x100 color image is stored as a 30000-element array where each triplet corresponds to red, green, and blue pixel values. On screen, display a small grid of pixels transforming into a matrix of numbers. Highlight one pixel and show its RGB values as a numeric triplet. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.

Next, compare the choices involved in Feature Detection and Calibration and make the decision criteria explicit. Feature methods locate and describe repeatable image patterns. Consider this worked case: SIFT features identify keypoints like corners and edges. Camera calibration maps real-world distances to pixel coordinates using known reference points. On screen, draw a grid of detected feature points on an image. Overlay a calibration grid showing how real-world distances map to image coordinates. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

Use Evaluation and Robustness Testing to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Evaluation tests sensitivity to viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Consider this worked case: An AI model is tested with images taken at different angles, under bright and dim light, with partial occlusions, and from different camera types. On screen, display a 2x2 grid of test images varying in viewpoint, lighting, occlusion, and data shift. Annotate each with the tested condition. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

Apply Geometric Transforms and Segmentation to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Segmentation assigns pixels or regions to selected categories. Consider this worked case: Perspective transform corrects a tilted photo. Foreground segmentation isolates moving objects from a static background. On screen, show a distorted image transforming into a straight, aligned image. Highlight segmented regions with different colors. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.

Begin by framing Foundations of AI System Architecture as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.
